newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-San Mig's pork-to-property move hailed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-San Mig's pork-to-property move hailed.

text.p: Food and beer giant San Miguel Corp's decision on Thursday to set aside its meat and livestock business in favour of property development was welcomed by analysts who hailed the move as a wise strategic decision.

"It's a good move...The significance of this is that it's getting rid of the low-return business and focus on business that will get higher returns," Norman Villamin, research head of UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd, said.
Nothwithstanding the fears of a property glut, he said, earnings prospects in property development could easily outshine the bleak outlook for the livestock and poultry industry.

Rachelle Regala, a food and consumer analyst at HSBC James Capel, said a stronger property business would offset the company's declining profits in its core food and beer business which is suffering from higher raw material costs and excess capacity.
San Miguel announced on Thursday it would spin off the main operation of its Monterey Farms Corp to another unit.
San Miguel Properties Philippines Inc (SMPPI), with total real estate assets amounting to 15.2 billion pesos ($578 million), would be merged with Monterey, the company said.
Monterey owns property assets worth 1.2 billion pesos.
The move to merge the property unit into Monterey was a virtual "backdoor" listing.
"The merger will provide San Miguel's real estate business with a vehicle to access the equity capital market in the future to finance its redevelopment projects," San Miguel said.
A backdoor listing refers to companies taking over listed firms and gaining access to the equities market without going through the cumbersome requirements for listing.
The move, hailed for the benefits it would bring to San Miguel, sent analysts scrambling to their files as the backdoor listing was through a stock hardly ever traded.
Most said it was too early to predict how Monterey's stock would react on Friday.
Monterey's last deal was done at 90 pesos a share on April 22 and until more information was available on its assets, it was difficult to say if its present price was undervalued, analysts said.
A severe lack of liquidity in the stock meant it would be difficult to buy, they said.
Analysts estimated San Miguel held 93 percent of the stock. ($1 = 26.30 pesos)
